Second thing is, if we just say, well, OK, even though these four remaining claims are based on a mix of communications, some of them are protected, some of them aren't, even though the defendants didn't really explain, we're just going to go ahead and lump everything together and assume that these are potentially protected. Here's where we get to the commercial speech exemption. And the trial court, this was another basis for the trial court's order denying the motion to dismiss. Basically said that to the extent that any of the claims are based on statements about AEG's products, and those could be potentially protected, those fall within the commercial speech exemption. Now, there's been a fair amount of writing on it. I think this much the parties agree on, and that is that this is a statutory exemption. It has been construed by the Texas Supreme Court in Castleman, and Castleman has imposed four requirements. But at the end of the day, there are actually a lot of cases.

So in the defendant's view, the commercial speech exemption only applies if the defendants make statements about the defendant's products to the defendant's own customers. And I would just say, A, that's not what Castleman says, and B, that doesn't make any sense. Because if that's all that's happening, the plaintiff hasn't been injured. The plaintiff's not even involved in this transaction. So the reality is the statements just have to be about the kind of products the defendant sells. In this particular instance, what distinguishes this case from Castleman, and I think is really sort of the key point in the analysis, is that both AEG and WMI are engaged in the same industry. They are competitors for some of the same customers. And so in this instance, statements made to one potential customer is the equivalent of a statement made to another potential customer. A lot of the distinctions that you get from Castleman, frankly, don't matter. Bottom line is, because they're competitors in the same industry, because the pleadings and the evidence suggest that the statements were made to actual or potential customers of both parties, and because the statements were made to advance WMI's own business interests, I think that this is clearly a case where, if the court gets that far, it would do what the trial court did and say, you know what? The rest of the claims, to the extent they're based on statements about products, the commercial speech exemption applies. And I've exceeded my time.
